### `found-30-sep/comment-file-index-only-in-a-migration` — **closed** (schema, small; found closing `found-30-sep/attachments-unordered`)

**The index on a task file's comment exists only where 0043 ran**

*Evidence, 30 September, read, not measured on a migrated database:* 0043 creates `task_attachments_comment_id_idx`, and the drizzle schema does not declare it. The pristine dump, the schema reference, the lanes and CI are built by push and have no such index; a database migrated through 0043 has it. The drift gate compares a lane with the push-built reference, so it cannot see this.

*To close:* declare it in the schema (and push it to the lanes), or drop it by a migration, then look for other indexes that live in a migration only.

*Closed, 30 September,* for every index and check, not only this one. Production runs `drizzle-kit migrate`, which reads the migrations. The lanes, CI and a fresh deploy run `drizzle-kit push`, which reads only the schema.

Measured first:
- A reader over the 172 migrations, in the journal's order, was compared with the schema source. The migrations leave 22 indexes and 11 checks that the schema does not declare.
- Three of the indexes are unique: `uq_projects_default_container_per_space` (0129), `uq_object_shares_email` (0085) and `uq_workspace_groups_alias` (0090).
- The checks: 0036's status scope, 0039's channel notification level, 0085's one principal per share, 0090's presence and time-off range, 0134's view visibility, 0136's space default permission, 0140's two AI value bounds, 0141's calendar provider and 0150's AI run status.
- Unique constraints, tables and foreign keys were compared the same way. Every foreign key a migration makes (160) is declared, with the same ON DELETE. Every unique constraint is declared. One table is not (below).

What it cost, measured:
- Lanes 3 and 4 held rows that production refuses. Three spaces each had two hidden list containers, made 60–170 ms apart on 23–25 September. One view had the visibility "everybody".
- On lane 5 with the index dropped, `list-under-space`'s new check made six lists at once in a new space. That made six containers, and the space listed one of the six lists. With the index there was one container, and all six were listed.

What changed:
- 21 indexes and 11 checks are declared in 20 schema files, each under the name and definition its migration gives it.
- `idx_docs_public_share_id` is not declared. It duplicated `docs_public_share_id_unique` on the same column, so 0171 drops it, and a migrated database and a pushed one hold the same indexes.
- The definitions were compared on scratch databases, both built from the pristine dump. One is the old push plus the migrations' own statements. The other is a push of the new schema. They describe the same (`schema_describe`, 2379 lines each, no difference), and their 458 index and constraint names are the same.
- The lanes: on lanes 3 and 4, the extra containers were folded into the first (their lists moved with them) and the stray view was removed. The indexes and checks were put on lanes 1–7 and the pristine database, and the reference was rebuilt from the new source. Lanes 1–7 report no drift. Lanes 8–10 were already behind (no `announcement_views`, among others) and are not running.

Checks:
- `check-schema-declares-migrations.mjs` reads the migrations in the journal's order, and the schema. It fails on anything a migration leaves that the schema does not declare by name: an index, a check or unique constraint, or a table.
- It also fails on anything the schema declares that no migration makes, unless the baseline made it. The baseline is 39 tables and 19 names, declared in 2e31089 with migrations 0000–0009, on tables no migration creates; production has them from its first push.
- A column that a migration writes `UNIQUE` counts as declared by `.unique()` on that column. 0048's webhook token is one: Postgres calls it `inbound_webhooks_token_key`, and a push calls it `inbound_webhooks_token_unique`.
- Before, the gate found 33 differences; after, none. `check-schema-declares-migrations-cases.mjs`: 24 cases hold, and 21 of 21 mutations bite. Both run in preflight and in CI's verify job.
- `list-under-space` has a 14th check: six lists made at once share one container, and all six are listed. It fails 13/14 without the index and passes 14/14 with it (lane 5). The suite then deletes the space it raced in, by SQL, so a lane without the index keeps no extra containers.
- `lus-4` removes the index from the schema. The break runner measured it at `f335b89` (lane 1): 13/14 against 14/14, reddening the new check.
- Regression on lanes 5 and 7: the 20 suites that read or write these tables, all green, 461 checks (`list-under-space` 14, `view-visibility` 23, `share-levels` 6, `calendar-accounts` 37, `meeting-tags` 4, `public-doc-page` 12, `folder-dialog` 29, `status-write-access` 4, `doc-trash-level` 5, `user-group-access` 8, `ai-value` 23, `ai-activity-filters` 34, `settings-depth` 62, `person-panel` 60, `container-delete-keys` 10, `archived-tasks-access` 7, `chat-message-actions` 73, `goal-access` 13, `teams-destination` 14, `task-attachments` 23).

Found while closing it: `found-30-sep/task-labels-left-in-production`.

Not measured here: production itself. Every index and check above is one that production already has from its migrations. 0171 is the only change it will see.

### `found-30-sep/unit-claims-refuse-an-uncommitted-batch` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found closing `found-30-sep/comment-file-index-only-in-a-migration`)

**Preflight's unit-claims step fails every batch that changes `apps/` or `packages/` before it is committed**

*Evidence, 30 September:* `check-unit-claims.mjs` ends by asking `git status --porcelain -- apps packages`, and fails on any line, so that a break patch left applied is caught. A batch under test has lines there by definition. The step failed on this batch (the 20 schema files and 0171) and on batches 145–148, each time with every claim reddening (110 of 110 here), and each commit message has had to explain it. A patch left applied on top of an uncommitted batch reads the same as the batch alone, so the step cannot tell them apart.

*To close:* compare the tree with its own state before the first patch, as a run from elsewhere already does for the main checkout, rather than with HEAD. Add a case and a mutation.

*Closed, 30 September.* `lib/tree-state.mjs` takes a state of apps and packages: the status lines, a digest of the diff against HEAD, and a digest of every untracked file's name and bytes. `check-unit-claims.mjs` takes one before the first patch and one after the last, and fails only when they differ, naming what moved. By content, not by status: a file the batch had already changed reads ` M` before and after, whether or not a patch was left on it, so a comparison of status lines alone would have let exactly that through.

Checks:
- `check-tree-state-cases.mjs` plants git repositories: 9 cases hold, and 6 of 6 mutations bite.
- The four cases that must read as not moved: a clean tree, an uncommitted batch left as it was (the case the old check failed every time), a staged change written again with the same bytes, and a change outside apps and packages.
- The five that must read as moved: a clean file with a patch left on it; a file the batch changed, changed again, whose status reads the same; a staged file with a patch left in the working tree; an untracked file of the batch rewritten; a file a patch made and left.
- Before, preflight's step failed on this batch and on batches 145 to 148 with every claim reddening. After, it passes on this batch, with its apps and packages uncommitted, in the preflight below. The cases run in preflight and in CI's verify job.

### `found-30-sep/drift-reads-only-committed-changes` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found closing `found-30-sep/unit-claims-refuse-an-uncommitted-batch`)

A file among the paths that did not exist then, untracked now, is named as changed too. So a batch that grows a suite reads that suite's logs as drifted before it is committed, as they read after, and the planner and the reddened checker agree on it either way.

### `found-30-sep/access-asks-from-outside-the-workspace` — **closed** (security, small; found closing `found-30-sep/private-task-reads-say-403`) · reproduced 5 October

**Any account asks any workspace's admins for access, by the workspace's id**

*Evidence, 30 September, lane 2, before and after this work:* a user of another organisation, a member of no part
of the workspace, sends `POST /shares/task/<an open task's id>/request {workspaceId}`. The answer is 201, the ask is
recorded in the workspace's `content_access_requests`, and every admin is notified "… asked for access to <the task's
title>". The route asks nothing of the asker. Its comment says "It needs only a workspace membership, which the
service establishes by looking the object up inside `workspaceId`", and the service does not do that. ClickUp does
let people outside a workspace request access ("People outside your Workspace must request access to a public or
private item", help centre excerpt), but approving such an ask there is an invitation with its own permission. Here
nothing checks the asker at all, and a workspace's id reaches whoever holds any of its links.

*To close:* decide whether an outsider may ask.
- If so, name the approval path and limit asks per asker.
- If not, answer a non-member 403, in the same words for every workspace id (as the guard's named-workspace answer).
- Check it with an outsider beside a member.

*Triage, 5 October, after the revert:* reproduced on a lane. Any signed-in account outside a workspace still gets 201 for an access ask there: the ask is recorded and every admin is notified (lane 1). Whether outsiders may ask at all is still the owner's decision. Whether someone outside the workspace may ask at all is still the owner's decision; the defect counted is that nothing checks the asker, so any account notifies every admin about any id, and the answer tells whether a workspace id is real. Evidence: `docs/triage-2026-10-05.md`.

*Closed, 7 October* (lane 3). ClickUp lets people outside a Workspace ask for an item by its link: "People outside your Workspace must request access to a public or private item", and those who may approve are the item's owner and whoever may invite guests (help centre, "Request and approve access to Workspace items", through search excerpts; the site is blocked here). So anyone signed in may still ask, and the approval path is the object's Share panel, which the notice links to, for those it tells: the object's admins and the workspace's.

- An ask is only about something that is there. The object must be one of the named workspace's (`resolveSharedBatch`, the read the notice's title already made, now made first). A made-up id, a workspace that is not there, or another workspace's object is one 404, "There is nothing by that link to ask for access to", the same for each; nothing is recorded or sent. So no answer tells whether a workspace id, or an object, is real.
- One person's asks are capped at 20 an hour, about anything, anywhere (`ACCESS_ASKS_PER_HOUR`). The next is refused 429, "You have asked for access too many times in the last hour — try again later", recorded nowhere and told to nobody. Asking about the same object again within the day is still "already asked", as before, and costs nothing.
- The card on a refused page said "sent" whatever came back (`onSettled`), so a refused ask read as one passed on. It now says a refusal in the server's words (`request-access-refused`).

Measured on lane 3 (`access-probe.mjs`), an account in no part of the workspace asking:

- After: the real task 201 "sent", one told; the four others 404 in the same words; the thirty made-up ids 404 each. 1 ask recorded, 1 notice.
- `request-access` on lane 3 before the API changed: 10 of 12, the two refusal checks red; after, 12 of 12. Its card check on the bundle before, against lane 3's API: the card said "sent" after the 429, 12 of 13; on this bundle, 13 of 13.

### `found-30-sep/lanes-save-downloads-in-ascii` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found closing `found-30-sep/list-export-saved-as-list-csv`) · reproduced 5 October

**On the lanes, Chromium saves any download named outside ASCII as "download", so no suite can see a name in another script unless it asks for a UTF-8 locale**

*Evidence, 30 September:*
- The lanes' shells set no `LANG`. Under the POSIX locale Chromium converts a download's name to ASCII, and falls back to "download" when it cannot.
- Measured with a bare page: "Übersicht 1.csv", "قائمة 1.csv" and "a — b.csv" were each saved as "download".
- Under `LANG=C.UTF-8` each was saved as named. GitHub's runners are UTF-8, so CI and the lanes measure different things.
- `list-export` and `file-exports` now launch with `utf8LocaleEnv()`. `task-attachments` names its zip in ASCII, and every other suite's browser still runs in the POSIX locale.

*To close:* give every suite's browser a UTF-8 locale: `launchOptions()` passes `env`, or `lane_*_env` exports `LANG`. Then check Download all's zip saved under a title in Arabic.

*Triage, 5 October:* reproduced on a lane. On the lanes, Chromium still saves any non-ASCII download name as "download" unless the suite passes utf8LocaleEnv(), and only two suites do. Evidence: `docs/triage-2026-10-05.md`.

*Closed, 6 October* (lane 2). The lanes' runners start every suite in a UTF-8 locale, as GitHub's runners and a reader's desktop have: `verify.sh` and `wt-break.sh` run each suite under `env "${LANE_SUITE_LOCALE[@]}"` (`LANG=C.UTF-8 LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `lane-env.sh`), which the suite's browser inherits, so a download named in any script is saved under its name on a lane as well. Only the suite's process is given it; the lanes' APIs are started as before. Under it the browser's language, its `Intl` locale, its date and number formats and its collation read as they did (`en-US`, a bare page measured both ways); only the charset is UTF-8. `utf8LocaleEnv` stays, for a suite started by hand from a shell with no locale.

Measured on lane 2 with the extended `task-attachments` suite: before, through `verify.sh` as it was, the task retitled "ملفات المراجعة <tag>" had its zip saved as "download" (33 of 34, the new check red); after, as "ملفات المراجعة <tag>-attachments.zip" (34 of 34; 34 of 34 again in the regression sweep, on lane 7).

Checks:
- `task-attachments` 33 → 34: a task titled in Arabic has its zip saved under that title, not as "download".
- `verify-guards-selfcheck.sh` holds the runners to it: a suite started from a shell with no locale runs in UTF-8 (`locale charmap`, read as Chromium reads its charset), and each line of `verify.sh` (one) and `wt-break.sh` (two) that starts a suite starts it so. With `--mutate`, no locale and a `verify.sh` line without it are each caught, from a shell with no locale and from a UTF-8 one, as CI's runner is.
- Patches `tat-13` (the zip's name is sent in ASCII alone, with no `filename*`) and `tat-14` (the page never reads `filename*`) each redden it: the browser saved "<tag>-attachments.zip". Until now only the unit claims of `dla-21` and `dla-22` could see either.

Found while closing it:
- `found-7-oct/a-tab-that-saw-the-sign-out-misses-the-sign-in`: in this batch's regression `session-in-the-browser` failed, and it fails as often without the locale as with it.

### `found-30-sep/a-hung-page-outlasts-every-wait` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found running `task-attachments`' break set at `7751d5a`)

**A wait whose question never answers waits for ever, whatever its timeout says**

*Evidence, 30 September, lane 1:* the break runner's baseline of `task-attachments` at `7751d5a` printed "▶ the panel, frame `01:55`" at 12:18:41, then nothing for fourteen minutes, until it was stopped. The lane's API saw the signed-in page open its socket and close it at 12:18:54, as the page left for the task's address, and then no request at all. Every wait in that section has a timeout of 30 s or less. `waitUntil` (`test/e2e/lib/wait.mjs`) awaits its predicate before it looks at the deadline, so a predicate that never settles holds it for ever. The likeliest such predicate is a Playwright call to a page whose renderer stopped answering: an agent had measured 5.4 GB free with no swap half an hour before, with three browsers and a preflight running. Read, not proven: the run left no trace of which call it was in. The suite ends only at its runner's 900 s kill, reported as one failed check. 151 suites call `waitUntil`, 1,072 times. The same suite passed 32/32 on lane 5, at the same code, half an hour earlier.

*To close:* race each predicate against the time left, and count one still pending at the deadline as a no. `waitForCount` goes through `waitUntil`; `textOf`, whose `page.evaluate` has no timeout, needs the same. Check it with a predicate that never settles: the wait returns false at its deadline.


*Closed, 30 September.* `waitUntil` races each look against the time left (`settledWithin`, `test/e2e/lib/wait.mjs`). A look still pending at the deadline, plus a grace, counts as no, and the wait gives up. A throw is still a reason to look again.
- The grace is 15 s (`LAST_LOOK_GRACE_MS`, and `lastLookGraceMs` per call), because predicates wait inside themselves. Across the 1,072 calls, the longest such wait is 8 s (`comment-slash-commands`), and `list-export` runs two 5 s waits back to back. Every predicate that answers at all still answers as before. One that never does costs its deadline plus 15 s instead of the run.
- `waitForCount` goes through it. `textOf` gives a page that never answers 5 s a look, eight looks, then reads it as empty.
- `scripts/check-wait-helper.mjs` states the contract in 15 assertions: a predicate that never settles, or stops answering part-way, is a no at the deadline; a true one is a yes, and a false one a no no sooner than the deadline; a look begun before the deadline that answers within the grace counts; a throw is looked past; the default grace outlasts the longest wait inside a predicate; and the same for `waitForCount` and `textOf`. Each case that could hang runs under its own watchdog, so a mutant that waits for ever fails a named case.
- Against the committed helper, 7 of 15 fail: the five that hang, and the grace. With it, 15 of 15 hold, and 7 of 7 mutations fail a case (the race removed, a pending look read as yes, the deadline never read, no grace, a throw read as the end, a 2 s grace, `textOf` without its bound). The check runs in preflight and CI.
- Regression on lane 6 with the new helper: `comment-slash-commands` 10, `list-export` 30, `task-menu` 37, `folder-dialog` 29, `chat-message-actions` 73, `task-header-status` 15 and `video1-fast-items` 92 (the suites whose predicates wait longest inside themselves), `menu-reopen` 26 three times and three more, all green, 427 checks.

### `found-30-sep/schema-reference-reads-the-main-tree` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found closing `found-30-sep/attachments-unordered`)

**A worktree with a migration is refused by its own `fleet-restart.sh`, and working round it can rebuild the shared reference**

*Evidence, 30 September:* `schema_ref_ensure` (`lane-env.sh`) keys and builds its reference from `/home/user/rundesk`, whichever checkout calls it. A lane served from a worktree whose migration adds an index reads as drift ("extra: index task_attachments …") and is refused. The way round, used here and by `ledger-rows/row-850` before it, is a reference of the worktree's own in `SCHEMA_REF_DIR`, keyed to the main tree's hash. If the main tree's schema changes while such a reference is in use, the key stops matching, and `schema_ref_ensure` rebuilds into that directory, from the main tree, into the shared database name `rundesk_schema_ref`, under a lock held in that directory only, so two shells can rebuild the shared database at once.

*To close:* build and key the reference from the calling checkout, name its database after its directory, and check both with a worktree that adds an index.

*Closed, 30 September.* Measured first: a planted checkout (the lane scripts beside a copy of `packages/db` whose schema declares one index more, as a worktree with a migration would) asked `lane_schema_drift` about lane 5, which lacks that index. It read no drift (rc 0). The reference it used was the main checkout's, built and keyed from `/home/user/rundesk`, and held no such index.
- The reference is now the calling checkout's. `schema_ref_root` is the checkout `lane-env.sh` lives in. The main checkout keeps `/tmp/claude-0` and `rundesk_schema_ref`, so nothing changes for it: its key and its reference database are the ones the lanes were already checked against. Any other checkout, and any `SCHEMA_REF_DIR`, gets a directory and a database named after it (`schema_ref_dir`, `schema_ref_db`). So two references never share a database, and never build it under two locks.
- `schema-drift-selfcheck.sh` plants such a checkout. 10 of 10 hold, four new: it builds its own reference under its own name, with its index in it; it reads a database without that index as drift, naming the index; this checkout's reference keeps its key and still reads the same database as no drift; and a reference kept in another directory gets a database of its own. The planted database and directories are removed at the end.
- The script is renamed over the old one, so a shell sourcing it mid-edit reads one whole version.

### `found-30-sep/suite-runs-leave-accounts-behind` — **closed** (test tooling, medium; found closing `found-30-sep/templates-null-array-field-values`)

**Suites leave the people they sign up, and the workspaces and spaces they "delete", on every run, not only a killed one**

*Evidence, 30 September, lane 6:*
- One clean run of each suite left behind:
  - `template-center`: the two people it signs up, with their organizations and personal workspaces. It takes them out of the shared workspace, but their accounts stay.
  - `project-template-key`: three accounts and organizations, its workspace (archived, not deleted) with its two saved templates, and a custom role.
  - `like-literal` and `role-permissions-web`: their accounts (two each, with organizations and personal workspaces) and their own workspace, archived.
  - `space-default-permission`: its account, organization and personal workspace.
  - `template-center`'s applied space, `space-default-permission`'s five spaces and `space-create-menu`'s space: archived in the shared Main Workspace.
- This session's runs left 34 accounts, 34 organizations, 42 workspaces and 18 archived shared-workspace spaces. They were removed by hand.
- Before it, lane 6 already held 627 `@rundesk.invalid` accounts (114 of them `tc-`), 292 archived workspaces, and 148 archived spaces in Main Workspace out of its 158.
- `create-modal-templates` shows how to clean up: it deletes its workspace by id and its member's own organization, membership and account.

It is the wider form of `found-30-sep/killed-suites-leave-members-behind`: most of what is left is left by runs that ended well.

*To close:* have each suite delete what it made, as `create-modal-templates` does: accounts, their organizations, and workspaces and spaces removed rather than archived. Sweep tagged leftovers at the start of a run, and check that a run leaves no row it made.


*Closed, 30 September.* Measured first on lane 6, one clean run each on `f532edc`: `template-center` left 2 accounts, 2 organizations, 2 workspaces and an archived space in Main; `project-template-key` 3, 3 and 4 (one archived) with 2 templates and a custom role; `like-literal` and `role-permissions-web` 2, 2 and 3 (one archived) each; `space-default-permission` 1, 1, 1 and five archived spaces in Main; `space-create-menu` an archived space and a form in Main. The lane held 651 `@rundesk.invalid` accounts, 389 archived workspaces, and 153 archived spaces in Main of 164.
- One registry for every suite, `test/e2e/lib/made.mjs`. `signUpApi` registers each person before asking for them. `apiAs` registers what `POST /workspaces`, `/spaces`, `/lists` and `/invitations` make. A suite registers anything else with `madeRow`. Each registration goes into a journal on disk before the call returns.
- When a run ends, `made-sweep.mjs` deletes what its journal names, by SQL: the rows; the organizations only its accounts own, made since the run began; the notifications its accounts caused; then the accounts made since the run began (an older one, registered by mistake, is kept and said). The product has no route that deletes an account or an organization. A row left behind is named and fails the run. An account made during the run that no run registered is named too.
- 21 suites that made people by a raw route register them, and eight more register a form, invitations, docs, tasks, time blocks or an account made through a page. `check-suite-made-registered.mjs` refuses a suite that makes an account without a registration of its own before the request (31 sites in 21 suites) — an arrow with no braces or a loop that makes accounts, with its registration only outside it, among them — and a `signUpApi` that stops registering (29 cases, 19 of 19 mutations bite). `check-made-sweep.mjs` runs probe processes against Postgres (24 cases, 21 of 21 mutations bite). Both are in CI.
- The sweep refuses a journal that says no start (its name does not parse and it has no `{"run":{"started":…}}` line): the start is what keeps the admin and older organizations out of it. A run whose first registered row is not in the database it cleans (`DATABASE_URL` is not the API's) stops there, removes nothing, sets its list aside and exits 1 saying how to sweep it where the rows are; a journal none of whose rows is in the database, whose run never saw it hold one, is refused the same way.
- After, on lane 6: each of the six suites, three runs in a row and once more on `bac7eae`, added no account, organization, workspace, space, member, template, role, invitation or form, and no other row but the admin's sessions, rate-limit counters and Main's audit trail. All passed, as did the 21 converted suites and nine more (one run of `auth-route-limits` met a sign-up window the suites before it had spent, and passed alone).

Found while closing it: `found-30-sep/suite-cleanup-leaves-stored-objects`, `found-30-sep/lanes-hold-earlier-runs-leftovers` and `found-30-sep/suite-leftovers-unmeasured`.
- Merged here onto `2d38c0e` (one clash: `request-access` had moved onto `signUpApi` in the batch before, which now registers each person, so that side was kept). The gate names none over the 262 suites, and 19 of 19 mutations bite; it and its cases run in preflight too. Run again on lanes 2, 4, 5 and 7: the 25 suites this changed and `sign-in-and-password`, all green, 456 checks, and the four named suites it changed through `signUpApi` alone (`project-template-key`, `like-literal`, `role-permissions-web`, `space-default-permission`) 5, 5, 5 and 36, all green. `check-made-sweep.mjs` against lane 6: 24 cases hold, and 21 of 21 mutations bite (a first run cut off by a 15-minute limit of mine left one mutant file beside its subject, removed).

### `found-30-sep/template-values-written-unchecked` — **closed** (visible bug, small; found closing `found-30-sep/templates-null-array-field-values`)

**A template's one-value custom field is written onto the new task unchecked, whatever the same-named field there is**

*Evidence, 30 September, read and not yet measured:*
- `fitTemplateValue` now checks a list against the target field: members, options, tasks, never votes or files.
- A one-value field is still written "as it always was": into whichever field of that name the list's project has.
- So a template saved from one project writes text into another project's Number field, an option its Dropdown does not define, or an address into an Email field the route would refuse.
- The field's own route (`CustomFieldsService.setValue`) refuses each of these with 400.

*To close:* check a template's one-value values as the route does, with the route's validation shared rather than copied. Check it with a template applied in a project whose same-named field has another type or other options.

*Closed, 30 September* (built by an agent on lane 4). ClickUp's help centre says nothing of a template applied where a field of the same name takes another kind of value; of a template's fields it says only "If you choose to include Custom Fields, Formula Fields will not be included" ("Use List templates"). Its own API refuses a value that is not one of a field's options: "Values must each be a valid option id" (quoted in a Zapier community thread). So a value is written only where the field's own route would take it, and the rest are still written.

Measured first on lane 4: a template holding the words "about a week", the option "critical", the words "the front desk" and a note, applied in a project whose fields of those names are a Number, a Dropdown of Low and High, an Email and a Text field, wrote all four, where the route refused the first three (400 each), in three runs of three.
- The route's validation moved, unchanged, from `CustomFieldsService.setValue` into `checkValue`, which `setValue` calls and whose answer it stores. The text is the same, so the patches anchored in it still apply, and the six whose anchors lie inside it still redden their checks.
- Every value a template writes onto a task is asked of `checkValue`, after `fitTemplateValue` has fitted a list to its field. A value it refuses is not written; the rest are.
- Nothing yet tells the person which were left out (`found-30-sep/template-leaves-values-out-silently`).

Checks: `create-modal-templates`, 20 → 23. A second project with the four fields, the route asked each value on a task there, and the task made from the template read by SQL: "a template’s words, applied where the field of that name is a Number, leave that field unset — as the field’s own route refuses them (400), read by SQL", "and its option, where that field is a Dropdown without it, leaves the Dropdown unset — as its route refuses it (400)" and "and words that are no address, where that field is an Email field, leave it unset — as its route refuses them (400) — while the Note, a Text field there too, is written".
- Before, the three failed in three runs of three. After, 23/23 in six runs, three in a row each at `32bfebb` and `8c1b727`.

The break runner measured `tvu-1`, `tvu-2` and `tvu-4` again at `f335b89` (lane 1): 23, 23 and 25 of 26 against 26/26.

**Duplicate copies a Voting field's votes and a Files field's attachment ids onto the copy**

### `found-30-sep/duplicate-reads-what-its-caller-cannot` — **closed** (security, small; found closing `found-30-sep/duplicate-copies-votes-and-files`)

**Duplicate copies a task its caller may not open, and hands them its words**

*Evidence, 30 September, measured on lane 4 by the agent and on lane 5 here:* `POST /workspaces/:ws/task-templates/duplicate/:taskId` asked workspace membership (`WorkspaceMemberGuard`) and, through `createTask`, the right to make a task in the list. It never asked the task's read rule. `POST …/task-templates/from-task/:taskId` snapshotted a task the same way, behind `template.manage` alone.

*To close:* ask the task's read rule before snapshotting, in both routes. Check that a member refused a task can neither duplicate it nor save it as a template (404, nothing made), while one who may open it can.

*Closed, 30 September.* ClickUp copies what its user can see: a task you may not open is not in front of you to duplicate or save, and a read of a task one may not open answers as a task that is not there, as every such read here does.
- Measured first on lane 5, with the trio's build: an admin's task, made private by SQL, was refused to a plain member (403 on `GET /tasks/:id`). The member duplicated it (201), and the copy held its description, "Hidden words …". Granted Manage templates by a custom role, the same member saved it as a template (201), and the template held the same words.
- Both methods now ask `readableTask` for the caller (`assertTaskOpenTo`) before they read the task, and answer 404 when it does not find the task for them. The controller passes the caller's account role with the id, as the other read rules take it.

Checks:
- `create-modal-templates`, 23 → 26: "a member refused a private task cannot duplicate it: 404, no copy is made, and none of its words come back"; "and granted Manage templates, cannot save it as a template: 404, and no template holds it"; and, so the refusals are about the task, "while a task they may open, the same member duplicates and saves as a template". Before: 24/26, the first two failing as above. After: 26/26.
- `task-templates.service.test.ts` has two new tests, one a route: each refuses a task the read rule does not find for its caller and makes nothing. The two tests that duplicate and save a task are scripted with the read rule's two reads. 29/29.
- `ddr-1` (Duplicate asks no read rule), `ddr-2` (Save as template asks none) and `ddr-3` (the rule refuses everyone) are aimed at the three checks. The break runner measured them at `f335b89` (lane 1): each reddens its own, 25/26 against 26/26. `ddr-4` and `ddr-5` are their unit claims.

### `found-30-sep/template-values-find-fields-by-name-alone` — **closed** (visible bug, small; found closing `found-30-sep/template-values-written-unchecked`)

**A template's or a duplicate's value goes to whichever field of that name the project's query returns last**

*Evidence, 30 September, read and not yet measured:* `materialiseTemplateValues` maps names over every field of the project, including fields scoped to another list, and two fields may share a name (nothing forbids it; `checkedFormulaConfig` refuses a formula over two for that reason). So a value can be written into a field the new task does not have, or into the other of two same-named fields. A duplicate, which stays in its own list, still copies by name rather than by field.

*To close:* map only the fields the new task has (project-wide or its own list's), decide between same-named fields deliberately, and copy a duplicate's values by field; check with a same-named field scoped to another list.


*Closed, 30 September* (built by an agent on lane 7). ClickUp lets two fields share a name ("multiple custom fields called the same thing", read through search excerpts), and its templates carry their fields rather than their names. What a value written by name should do where two fields share it is not said, so the rule is this product's.

Measured first on lane 7, three runs alike:
- A template applied in one list wrote its value into a field of that name scoped to another list, which the task does not have. It also wrote into the list-scoped one of two fields sharing a name, leaving the project's own empty. Which of the two it took changed between runs: `create-modal-templates` passed its precedence check in two runs of three.
- A task holding two fields of one name, saved as a template and applied, or duplicated, answered 409 after making the task, which held neither value: both went into one field, and a task holds one value per field.

The fix:
- A value goes only into a field the new task has (`fieldIsOnList`), planned by `fieldsForTemplateValues`:
  - by the field it came from first, since a template or a duplicate taken from a task now names it (`fieldId`);
  - else by name: the one field, or of two the one scoped to the task's own list, or neither of two at the same reach;
  - each field once.
- A duplicate copies by field. The snapshot reads a task's values in the order the task shows its fields.
- The snapshot takes only the values of the fields the task has where it is now (`fieldIsOnTask`). A move leaves a task's value rows, so a task moved out of a field's list, or in from another project, still held values it no longer showed. Measured on lane 7 in three runs, each such value fell to a field of its name:
  - a duplicate showed the project's Stage holding the hidden value while the original showed it empty;
  - a template saved from the task held the value and wrote it the same way;
  - a task moved in from another project gave that project's Stage to this one's.

Checks:
- `create-modal-templates`, 33 → 41. A side list, and two Stage fields, one the side list's and one the project's, all read by SQL:
  - "a template’s value is not written into a field of its name scoped to another list…";
  - "and applied in the side list… the side list’s own…";
  - "a task holding two fields of one name, saved as a template and applied in its own list, gives each value back to the field it came from (read by SQL)";
  - "and applied in the other list… writes that field once, with the value taken from it";
  - "and a duplicate of that task copies each value into the field it came from, not both into one (read by SQL)";
  - "a task moved out of the side list keeps its value in the side list’s Stage, which it no longer shows — and a duplicate of it writes that value into no field, the project’s Stage of that name among them, while its Note is copied (read by SQL)";
  - "and saved as a template, it holds no value for that field — only the Note — and applied in the list writes none into the project’s Stage (read by SQL)";
  - "and a task moved in from another project, still holding that project’s Stage, is duplicated without it: nothing goes into this project’s Stage of that name, while the Owner it has here is copied (read by SQL)".
- Before: the first five, 34, 34 and 33 of 38. The last three, on this work before the review fix: 38/41 in three runs, exactly those three failing.
- After: 38/38 in nine runs, three in a row each at `6f8e02c`, `bac7eae` and `f44b647`. Then 41/41 in three runs and once more at `f44b647`.
- `task-templates.service.test.ts` has eight new tests, which the old service fails; the review's three also fail against this work's service before the review fix (38/41).
- `tvn-1..5` redden 2, 1, 3, 1 and 2 of the first five checks, each exactly the ones it names. `tvn-11..13` redden 3, 1 and 1 of the last three (38/41, 40/41, 40/41), each exactly the ones it names. `tvn-6..10` and `tvn-14..16` redden the unit tests they name.
- `dcv-1..4` were re-anchored on the moved code and redden as before: 58/60, 59/60 and 59/60, plus their unit test. `ddr-2` and `ddr-5` were re-anchored on the snapshot's new call: 40/41, its own check, and its unit test.
- Regression on lane 7: 17 suites and 401 checks, all green; after the review fix, `custom-field-progress` ×3 and six more suites once, all green. The API's unit tests: 1907/1907.
- Merged here onto `f44b647` with the other three builders' batches (one clash: `create-modal-templates` took checks from two of them, 33 → 45, and a `T5_ID` both had declared; three of the fields batch's unit tests scripted one read fewer than the task-writes batch now makes, and do now) and run again on lanes 2, 4, 5 and 7, 26 suites, all green, 552 checks: among them `custom-field-access` 6, `custom-field-types` 33, `create-modal-templates` 45, `template-center` 81, `ai-read-access` 5, `ai-task-reads` 4.

### `found-30-sep/field-definition-takes-a-foreign-list` — **closed** (security, small; found closing `found-30-sep/field-route-takes-another-projects-field`) · reproduced 5 October

**A field is defined with a list of another project, and a share on that list decides who may define it**

*Evidence, 30 September, measured on lane 7* (`found-probe.mjs`: three runs for the admin, the last two for the member):
- `createDefinition` stores the `listId` it is sent without asking that the list is the project's. An admin defined a field in a project, scoped to a list of another project: 201, the other project's list stored. No task has that field.
- `assertMayDefineFields` puts that list in the `within` steps it hands `assertSpaceLevel`, and the most specific grant decides. A member in a view-only space was refused a field on its project (403). The same member, holding an edit share on a list of another space, defined one there by naming that list (201).
- They cannot rename or delete it (those ask without a list).

*To close:* refuse a `listId` that is not a list of the project (as a list that is not there), in `createDefinition` and in the rule's `within`. Check the member's two answers (403 both) and the admin's refusal, and that a field scoped to the project's own list is still made.

*Triage, 5 October:* reproduced on a lane. Reproduced on lane 3. An admin defines a field in one project scoped to another project's list (201, stored). A member in a view-only space is refused a field there (403) but defines one by naming a list of another space that is shared with them at edit (201). Evidence: `docs/triage-2026-10-05.md`.

*Closed, 5 October* (built by an agent on lane 7). In ClickUp, a field made from a List view, Table view or task "is added to the Hierarchy location where the view or task is located" (help centre, "Create Custom Fields", read through search excerpts). A field belongs to its location, and a list belongs to its own project.

Measured first on lane 7 with the triage's probe, three runs alike:
- An admin defined a field in project ONE scoped to project TWO's list: 201, stored with ONE and TWO's list.
- A member in a view-only space was refused a field there with no list and with the project's own list (403 each, the space's reason).
- The same member defined one by naming a list of another space shared with them to edit: 201, stored.

What changed:
- `listOfProject` (`common/permissions/field-access.ts`) asks whether a list is one of the project's.
- `assertMayDefineFields` puts the list in `within` only when it is the project's own. A list of another project is no step on the way, so the project's and the space's answer stands.
- `createDefinition`, after the rule, refuses a `listId` that is not a list of the project, as a list that is not there: 404 "List not found in this project", nothing stored. So whoever may not define fields there hears the rule's 403 first, whatever list they name.
- Nothing on the web offers another project's list: the create modal's scope offers the chosen project's list, the task sheet sends a scope, and the list and project pages send none. A refusal reaches the existing toasts in the server's words.

After, three runs alike:
- The admin's field on TWO's list: 404 "List not found in this project", none stored.
- The own-list field: 201.
- The member: 403 three times, each with the space's reason.
- The view-only project holds no field.

Checks:
- `field-writes-by-level`, 5 → 7. The two new checks: "a member refused fields in a view-only space is refused one there with no list (403), and naming a list of another space shared with them to edit (403) — no step on the way to this project — the space’s reason both times, none made (read by SQL)" and "a field scoped to a list of another project is refused, the admin’s included, as a list that is not there (404 “List not found in this project”, none made, read by SQL) — while one scoped to the project’s own list is made, stored with that list". Before, 5/7 (201 each). After, 7/7 in three runs.
- `field-access.test.ts` is new, with four tests. `custom-fields.service.test.ts` has two more, for `createDefinition`.
- `fdl-1` (the rule takes the list as sent) reddens exactly the first check (6/7: the member's named list answered 404, past the space). `fdl-2` (the list stored as sent) reddens exactly the second (6/7). `fdl-3` and `fdl-4` redden the unit tests they name (3/4 and 6/7).
- `fwl-3` (defining asks nothing) reddens the first check as well, measured 4/7. Its claim now names it.

Regression on lane 7 after the review fix: 17 suites and 477 checks, all green; API unit tests 1960/1960, web unit files 36/36, both typechecks clean.

*Review fix, 5 October* (lane 7). Two reviewers found the rule's list step unfinished. Each case was measured on lane 7 with their probes, then the fixer's, three runs alike:
- Renaming and deleting asked the rule without the field's list, although `found-25-sep/field-values-written-by-readers` was closed saying they ask "on its list, for a list's field". A member shared a list to view, in a space they may edit, renamed and deleted its field, the value with it (200; 1 value → 0). ### `found-30-sep/public-cdn-url-makes-every-object-public` — **closed** (security, small; found closing `resume-defects/resume-7`)

**Where `R2_PUBLIC_URL` is a CDN domain, every stored object is readable by its address, so a members-only clip is only as private as its link**

*Evidence, 30 September:* `R2Service.getObjectUrl` returns `${R2_PUBLIC_URL}/<key>` whenever that is not the raw R2 API host. A clip's members-only link then answers with the object's permanent public address. The same is true of every attachment, avatar and logo. The default deployment signs, and so do the lanes and CI.

*To close:* decide whether private content may ever be served from a public domain. If not, sign it wherever the content is private (members-only clips, task attachments), whatever `R2_PUBLIC_URL` says, and check it with a lane that sets a public URL.


*Closed, 30 September, after review.*

ClickUp's answer to the same complaint is Private Attachment Links. Its feedback board asks three times for attachments "behind Workspace authorization". The setting is "available on all plans" and "requires that the person accessing a Workspace attachment is logged into that Workspace"; its attachment URLs are "an unguessable, randomized string of characters" (help centre, read through search excerpts).

Rundesk has no setting that makes an attachment public. Its keys are `<prefix>/<milliseconds>-<name>`, carried in every signed URL. Cloudflare: "When you connect a Custom Domain, your R2 bucket becomes publicly accessible." So signing what is handed out is not enough: nothing private may be in a bucket a public domain serves.

So:
- `R2Service.getObjectUrl` signs, whatever `R2_PUBLIC_URL` says. Every private caller went through it:
  - task files and cover;
  - clips (link and library);
  - call recordings;
  - chat files and emoji;
  - form uploads.
- The pictures on show (avatars, workspace logos) live in `R2_PUBLIC_BUCKET_NAME`. `bucketFor` chooses by key shape (`isPublicImageKey`), for every upload, read, signature, copy and delete.
- `publicObjectUrl` gives `${R2_PUBLIC_URL}/<key>` only when the key is a picture's, the pictures have their bucket, and the domain was seen not to serve `R2_BUCKET_NAME`. Otherwise it signs.
- `checkPublicDomain` runs at boot, before the first request, and hourly. It puts an object in `R2_BUCKET_NAME`, reads it at the domain unsigned, and deletes it.
- A domain that serves the private bucket is used for nothing and logged as an ERROR naming the bucket to disconnect it from.
- Pictures saved before are moved to their bucket on boot. A picture's listing and delete reach both buckets, so the purge misses nothing mid-move.
- `.env.example` and the production template say:
  - `R2_PUBLIC_BUCKET_NAME` and `R2_PUBLIC_URL` go together, both or neither;
  - never connect a domain to `R2_BUCKET_NAME`;
  - the pictures' bucket needs the same CORS rule.

Measured first:
- The reviewer's chain against the first fix, on its own store and API, 3 runs of 3:
  - a member removed from the workspace, who had once listed a task's files, was told the domain by the unauthenticated images route;
  - the domain served the file unsigned by its key.

### `found-30-sep/public-routes-unthrottled` — **closed** (security, small; found closing `resume-defects/resume-7`)

**The public routes are not rate-limited**

*Evidence, 30 September:* `GET /public/clips/:token` has no throttle, and neither do the public doc, portal and image routes. The only global guard is CSRF. A clip token is 192 random bits, so guessing is not the risk; a flood is.

*To close:* throttle the public routes per address, and check that a burst is refused with 429 while an ordinary viewer is not.

*Closed, 30 September* (built by an agent on lane 3, merged and measured again here). ClickUp documents limits for its API alone: "The ClickUp API applies rate limits per token", 100 requests a minute on Free Forever, Unlimited and Business, and "If you exceed the rate limit, the API returns a HTTP 429 status code" (developer docs, read through search results; the site is blocked here). Its help centre says nothing of limits on public links, Docs or Clips.

So the safe rule: what anybody may ask without an account is limited per address, the one key such a request has, far above one visitor and far below a flood. The budgets are `PUBLIC_ROUTE_LIMITS`, beside `RateLimitGuard`:
- A page, 120 a minute: a shared doc, a clip's link, a client portal, the status page and a custom domain's branding. Each is asked once per page load. A public form's read already had this budget.
- A picture, 1,200 a minute: ten times a page, because one page draws dozens of avatars and logos, for members too.
- Past it, 429 with a Retry-After, as sign-in's limits answer. The counter is the guard's own: per route, address and minute, shared by every replica.
- The machines' routes are not limited: the TLS proxy's ask, Stripe's and the inbound webhooks, the calendar feed, SCIM, Zapier and the health checks. Each is one caller for many, and a refusal loses a certificate, an event or a feed.
- The sign-in and invitation routes are as they were (`found-30-sep/register-unthrottled`).

Checks:
- `public-route-limits` is new, with 11 checks and nothing stubbed, registered in CI (247 in `postgres-harnesses`). It reads, on each of the six routes, a burst one past the budget refused with 429 and a Retry-After. It also reads another address (127.0.0.2) and another route still served, the visitor served again after the minute, and four machine routes answering 1,201 without a 429. Its bursts start as a fresh minute begins. It ends only once that minute has passed, since every suite on a lane asks from 127.0.0.1. Before, 2/11 on lane 3: every burst was served whole. After, 11/11.
- `public-route-limits.test.ts` is new, with 20 tests. Each public handler carries its policy behind the guard; the machines' routes carry neither. Driven with the real routes' metadata, the guard refuses the 121st open of a doc from one address, and nobody else.
- `prl-1..18` are new: 11 aimed at the suite and 7 unit claims, each reddening what it names (lane 3, baseline 11/11). `prl-3`'s first run found that a burst could land in a minute an earlier suite had asked in, which is why the bursts wait for a fresh one.
- Regression on lane 3, run straight after the new suite: `doc-boundaries` 17/17, `object-key-boundaries` 23/23, `clip-links` 19/19 (20/20 here, with the check the store stub made possible), `clip-created-card` 26/26, `stable-images` 6/6, `hook-portal-access` 11/11 and `public-doc-page` 12/12. None met a 429.

Found while building it: `found-30-sep/client-address-behind-nginx`, `found-30-sep/test-email-route-open`, `found-30-sep/register-unthrottled` and `found-30-sep/public-pages-read-429-as-gone`.
- Merged here and run again: `public-route-limits` 11/11 alone on lane 5, then on lanes 5 and 7 the seven suites that call the public routes, all green, 115 checks, none meeting a 429 (doc-boundaries 17, clip-links 20, public-doc-page 12, object-key-boundaries 23, clip-created-card 26, stable-images 6, hook-portal-access 11). Its suite moved onto lib/fixture.mjs's one client.

### `found-30-sep/store-stub-drops-object-metadata` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found closing `resume-defects/resume-7`)

**The lanes' store stub keeps no object metadata, so a clip's title and length read back wrong on every lane and in CI**

*Evidence, 30 September:* a presigned PUT carries `x-amz-meta-title` and `x-amz-meta-durationseconds`, and `scripts/e2e-lanes/s3-stub.mjs` stores only the bytes and the type. So a clip's title reads back as its file name and its length as 0, in the library, in search and on the clip page. Real R2 keeps them.

*To close:* keep and return the `x-amz-meta-*` headers in the stub, with a case in `check-s3-stub.mjs` and a mutation that reddens it. Then a suite may read a clip's title as it was recorded.

*Closed, 30 September.* Measured first: a presigned PUT does not carry its metadata as headers. The SDK's presigner hoists every `x-amz-meta-*` into the URL's query string (a probe presigned `title` and `durationseconds`: both were query parameters, and `host` was the only signed header). A PUT the API sends itself carries them as headers. The stub read neither.

- The stub keeps both: the query's `x-amz-meta-*` and the headers', names lowercased, as S3 answers them.
- HEAD and GET answer them as `x-amz-meta-*` headers. A value that is not printable ASCII is answered RFC 2047-encoded (`=?UTF-8?B?…?=`), as S3 answers such a value. A header could not carry it as it stands.
- A copy with `REPLACE` takes the request's metadata, and a plain copy keeps the source's, as S3 does.

Checks:
- `check-s3-stub.mjs` has four new cases against the real `R2Service`: HEAD answers what a presigned PUT carried in its URL; a value that is not ASCII comes back RFC 2047-encoded; a PUT's metadata headers are kept; a `REPLACE` copy does not keep the source's. 30 cases hold, and 29 of 29 mutations bite, six of them new (a PUT keeps nothing, the URL is not read, the headers are not read, HEAD does not answer, non-ASCII answered as sent, `REPLACE` keeps the source's).
- `clip-links` has a 20th check: the library calls a clip by the title it was recorded with. Before, 19/20 on lane 5: the library called it `1790736374973-Members_only_e2e-cliplinks-….webm`, its storage file name. After, 20/20, once the lane's stub was restarted on the new source (it reports the file's hash, which the lane scripts compare).
- Regression on lanes 5 and 7, the nine suites that store or read objects, all green, 179 checks (clip-links 20, clip-created-card 26, clip-library 2, clip-setup 14, object-key-boundaries 23, comment-recording 33, workspace-delete-for-good 5, task-cover 42, attach-on-create 14). `csl-26` (the library calls a clip by its file name) is new, aimed at the new check. The break runner measured it at cb21d14 (lane 2): 17/20 against 20/20, reddening the new check and the two that read the clip page's title.

Not measured here: whether R2 itself answers a non-ASCII metadata value RFC 2047-encoded, as S3 does. If it does, a clip titled with an accent would read back encoded in the library; the product reads `head.Metadata?.title` as it is.

### `found-29-sep/priority-readd-answers-a-ticked-off-row` — **closed** (visible bug, small; found closing `ledger-rows/row-850`)

**Adding a task that is on a list but ticked off says it was added, and it stays off the rail**

*Evidence, 29 September:* the unique index on (owner, workspace, task) holds one row, and the insert answers a duplicate with the row that is there. A ticked-off row does not stop the prompt, because a done task may be offered again. So pressing Add answers with the done row. The toast says "Task added to … Priorities." while the task stays off the open rail. The owner's own add behaved the same before `ledger-rows/row-850`, which only inherited it.

*To close:* find out from ClickUp what adding a task already done on a priorities list does, and make the add do that, whether reopening the row or saying it is done. Check it from the prompt and from the route.

*Closed, 29 September.* ClickUp's priorities point at tasks. A task finished stays listed until the toast that follows finishing it clears it ("When you mark a task as done, we'll now gently nudge you with a toast asking if you want to remove it from your priorities — one click, gone", the LineUp feedback thread that became Personal Priorities). So adding it after that is a new add. Here a ticked-off row has already left the rail, so adding its task again puts it back:
- The row opens again, moves to the end of the list, and records who added it this time and when (`insertPriority`). A row still open is answered as it was, unmoved.
- `people.service.test.ts` has two new tests, one for each case: 10 of 10 pass.
- `assign-to-priorities` has a new check: the owner ticks the task off, adds it again, and the row is read back from the database. Before the fix it failed, "still done, at 1 of 1, added by the first adder still". After it, the row is open, last, and added by the owner.
- `acp-30` (the done row answered as it was) is 24/25, reddening that check. `acp-33` is its unit claim: the new test fails, 9 of 10.
- Regression on lanes 5–7: 14 suites that read priorities, the Planner or the person panel, all green, 257 checks.

### `found-29-sep/priority-field-adds-to-nobody-else` — **closed** (feature, small; found closing `ledger-rows/row-850`)

**A task's Priority field cannot add it to somebody's priorities**

*Evidence, 29 September:* ClickUp's Priority field has "Add to Personal Priorities", with a person's avatar to pick. Here the only ways a task reaches a colleague's list are the prompt after assigning and the route. The task menu's Add to › Someone's Priorities is `ledger-rows/row-845`.

*To close:* the Priority field's menu offers the workspace's members (not to a guest), and posts to `POST /workspaces/:ws/people/:userId/priorities`, or to the caller's own list. Check it end to end, with the route's refusals said in words.

*Closed, 29 September.* ClickUp: "click on the Priority field for a task, click an avatar (your avatar is always displayed on the left), and search or select a user" ("View and add tasks to your Personal Priorities").
- A button beside the task's Priority field, "Add to Personal Priorities", opens the workspace's people: you first, then everybody else, narrowed by a search box.
- Choosing yourself adds the task to your own list. Choosing a colleague goes through the colleague route (`POST /workspaces/:ws/people/:userId/priorities`), with its rules and its refusals, and the same toast as the prompt, which opens their panel.
- A guest is offered their own list alone (`priorityPeople`). Your own add is split out of the prompt's, so the field adds to YOUR list even while the prompt after assigning offers a colleague's. Adding to one person's list no longer closes a prompt about somebody else.
- Four locales.
- `assign-to-priorities` has three new checks, 28 in all: the people offered, you first; a colleague chosen there has the task on their list, as added by you and not on yours; and choosing yourself puts it on yours. Each is read from the server by the task's id.

- After: 28/28 on lane 7.
- `use-priorities.test.ts` has three new expectations: you first, a guest only themself, and search by name.
- `acp-34` (the list never opens) is 25/28, reddening all three. `acp-35` (a colleague chosen there lands on your own list) and `acp-36` (you listed last) are each 27/28, reddening their own check. `acp-37` is the unit claim: a guest offered everybody fails its expectation.
- Regression on lanes 5–7: 17 suites that open the task sheet or read priorities, all green, 437 checks.

### `found-29-sep/ui-sweep-teardown-skips-the-press` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found by the break run for `15e2681`)

**ui-sweep pressed Saturday back only if the button said so the moment it was drawn, so a six-day week could stay behind**

*Evidence, 29 September:* the break set for `ui-sweep` on lane 3, beside three other break runs, stopped at its baseline, 106/107. The teardown found "Saturday left as aria-pressed=true". At the end of section 14 the suite read the Sat button once, as soon as the settings page had drawn it, and pressed it only if that read said "true". A button drawn before the week has loaded says "false", so the press was skipped and the shared workspace kept a six-day week for every run after it. The teardown's own read had the same hole the other way: a button read before the week loads also says "false".

*Closed, 29 September:*
- The press back is decided by what the server holds (`GET /workspaces/:id/work-schedule`, Saturday is ISO day 6). The button is waited for until it shows the six-day week, pressed, and the server is waited for until it no longer holds Saturday.
- The teardown's check asks the server as well as the button, and puts the week back through the API when the press failed, so a failed run no longer leaves the next one a six-day week.
- After: 107/107 on lane 3 beside three break runs, two regression runs and an agent's (load about 13). The failing run was the break set's baseline under the same kind of load; its set is queued again on the next commit.

### `found-29-sep/killed-mutants-outlive-their-run` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found committing `found-29-sep/stub-mutants-time-out-unnamed`)

**A mutant run ended by its timeout left its stub listening and its probe file in apps/api, and `git add -A` staged the probes**

*Evidence, 29 September:*
- Before this commit, `git add -A` had staged eleven `apps/api/.s3-stub-probe-<pid>.ts` files.
- Sixteen mutant stubs (`.s3-stub-mutant-*.mjs --port 9301…9661`) were still listening. The run that ended them had finished 46 minutes earlier; it was the 2 s check of the timed-out message.
- The cause: spawnSync's timeout signals the mutant alone, so its stub, its `tsx` probe and the probe file it names after its pid all outlived it. A mutant that throws before stopping its stub leaves the stub the same way.
- The stubs left behind held ports in the gates' own ranges.

*Closed, 29 September:*
- `scripts/lib/run-mutant.mjs` runs a mutant as the leader of its own process group. When the run returns, however it ended, the runner ends the group and removes what the caller says the child names after its pid.
- The two stub gates run their mutants through it, and so does `proveMutationsBite`, which 17 gates use.
- `.gitignore` keeps mutants and probes out of a commit.
- `check-run-mutant.mjs --mutate` is in preflight and CI. A run its timeout ends leaves nothing running and no file, and so does one that exits by itself. 6 cases; 5 of 5 mutations caught.
- Measured with the limit at 1.5 s, which ends every one of the S3 gate's 22 mutant runs. With the runner at `2c78436`, 22 stubs were still listening afterwards and 22 probe files were in apps/api. With this one, none were; all 22 runs said they had been ended. `git add -A --dry-run` staged none of the 22 probes once `.gitignore` held them.
- At full limits, the two gates bite 22 of 22 and 11 of 11 and leave nothing running.

### `found-29-sep/innertext-reads-hidden-leaves` — **closed** (test tooling, medium; found closing `checks-read-textContent-not-what-is-shown`)

**A check that reads an element's `innerText` still reads a hidden element's whole text**

*Evidence, measured 29 September in the lanes' Chromium:* `innerText` leaves out hidden text inside an element that is drawn, but an element that is itself hidden (`hidden`, `display: none`) answers with its whole text, as `textContent` does; only `visibility: hidden` answers empty. There are 252 `innerText` / `allInnerTexts` reads in 86 suites, and about 35 have a visibility check on the same line. A read of a leaf — a count, a chip, a label — that stands for "shown" cannot fail on a patch that hides the leaf rather than removing it. `task-menu`'s print checks read the printed id out of a copy that is hidden on screen by design, so they say what the copy holds, not what paper shows.

*To close:* measure which `innerText` reads decide a check that text is shown, and give `check-suite-text-reads.mjs` the same three outs for them (a message, a visibility guard on the read, a marker with a reason); convert; and read `task-menu`'s print checks under print media.

*Closed, 29 September.* Measured first, at `15e2681`, each suite lexed with its comments stripped: 266 `innerText` / `allInnerTexts` / `.innerText` reads in 90 suites (the ledger's 252 in 86, counted on an earlier tree), and 130 more through `readText(locator)`, which is `lib/wait.mjs`'s `innerText` and which no grep for `innerText` sees: 396 reads in 115 suites. 121 already had an out; 32 read the page's own body and 10 asked the same element's visibility first, both of which do read what is drawn. 197 decided a check that text is SHOWN with nothing on the read (counts, chips, toasts, labels, rows, panels, 6 of them `<option>`s), 10 asserted an absence, 1 was page code already guarded by its own box, and 25 sat in five suites other work was changing.

In the lanes' Chromium a hidden leaf (`hidden`, `display: none`) answers `innerText` with its whole text, `visibility: hidden` and a closed `<details>` answer empty, the body answers with only what is drawn, and Playwright counts no `<option>` as visible.

- `check-suite-text-reads.mjs --mutate` (preflight, and CI's verify job) reads `innerText`, `allInnerTexts`, the `.innerText` property and `readText(locator)` with the same three outs as `textContent`. The visibility guard has to be on the element read, not an ancestor (`<option>`s excepted, guarded on their select). For `innerText` alone, the page's body and the same element asked first (`isVisible()`, or a `waitFor` for it shown, gating the read) count as guards too. 42 planted cases; 28 of 28 mutations bite.

*Closed:* `verify.sh` prints every FAIL line and the count, names the whole log when the run failed, and keeps one log per suite and lane (`run-<suite>-lane<N>.log`). ### `found-28-sep/e2e-proxy-advertises-the-apis-keep-alive` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found by the flaky-suite work on `three-suites-fail-under-a-full-sweep`)

**The e2e proxy told clients to keep a socket for 72 s and closed it after 5, so a suite's own request after a pause died with "fetch failed"**

*Evidence, measured 28 September:* `test/e2e/lib/local-stack.mjs` serves the bundle and proxies `/api` to a lane, forwarding the API's response headers as they came, `Keep-Alive: timeout=72` among them, while its own `http.Server` closes an idle socket after Node's default 5 s. A client keeps a socket as long as it is told, so a suite's `fetch` through the proxy after a pause of 5–72 s went out on a socket the proxy had closed: with a stand-in API saying `timeout=72` and 6 s idle gaps, 1 of 4 requests died with `UND_ERR_SOCKET`. `list-empty-states`, `ai-answer-rendering` and `create-menu-ai` each recorded a `fetch failed` of this shape in sweeps, with nothing wrong in the API's log.

*Closed:* the proxy passes only end-to-end headers (`endToEndHeaders`, RFC 9110 §7.6.1): `Connection`, `Keep-Alive` and the other hop-by-hop headers — and any the `Connection` header names — describe the connection they arrived on and are not forwarded, so a client sees the proxy's own keep-alive. The same stand-in after: `timeout=5` advertised, 0 of 4 failed.
- `scripts/check-local-stack-keepalive.mjs --mutate` (preflight, and CI's verify job): three requests 6 s apart through the proxy, each advertising no longer a keep-alive than the proxy keeps; and a copy of the proxy that forwards the upstream headers, which it must catch ("advertised a 72 s keep-alive, and this proxy keeps 5 s").
- Every browser suite goes through this proxy. The sweep on lane 7 with it (`three-suites-fail-under-a-full-sweep`) passed 19/19, the three suites that had died with `fetch failed` among them (23/23, 51/51, 24/24).

### `found-28-sep/unit-claims-leave-a-patch-on-a-kill` — **closed** (test tooling, small; found stopping a preflight)

**A preflight stopped during "the unit claims redden too" left a break patch applied to the product, with a fresh time on the file**

*Evidence, 28 September:* the preflight was stopped during `check-unit-claims.mjs`. `apps/api/src/modules/tasks/tasks.service.ts` was left with a unit patch applied: the dependency read had lost its workspace condition. The patch also gave the file a new mtime, so every lane then refused its API build as stale (`verify.sh` exit 7). `video-regression` was refused that way in a sweep. The restore was a `finally`, which a signal skips. The file was restored by hand, with its old time.

*Fixed, 28 September:* `check-unit-claims.mjs` holds the files it is patching in `pending` and restores them, bytes and times, on SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP before exiting. A synchronous child (the unit run) finishes first, and then the restore runs.

*To close:* stop a run mid-patch and read the tree. It must be unchanged in content and in time. Not measured yet: the check patches the shared tree, and agents were editing it.

*Closed, 28 September, measured.* A run was started, and SIGTERM was sent while a patch was applied (`ai-containers.ts` modified). The run finished its 37 claims and exited 0. The tree was identical to before in the contents and times of every tracked file under `apps/` and `packages/`.

This works differently from what the fix first said. With a handler registered, node delivers the signal on its event loop, and the claims loop is synchronous. So the signal waits for the loop, and every file is restored by its own `finally`. Stopping this step now takes as long as the step; it no longer leaves a patch behind. The comment says so. SIGKILL still cannot be caught.

The full run on the clean tree: 37 of 37 unit claims redden, the five new ones included (`cla-12`, `cla-13`, `fcr-4`, `uga-13`, `uga-14`).

### `found-25-sep/task-sheet-offers-refused-edits` — **closed** (visible bug, medium; found closing `task-edits-narrower-than-clickup`)

**The task sheet offers every change to anybody who can open the task, and a comment-only or view-only reader is refused each one**

*Evidence, read not run:* `task-detail-sheet.tsx` gates no control on what the person may do: no capability read, no read-only state. Title, status, assignees, fields, dates, archive and delete are drawn for a reader whose space is view-only or comment-only, and each is refused by the API (403) after it is pressed. The project page had the same defect, closed by asking the API (`GET /projects/:id/capabilities`, `found-24-sep/project-page-offers-guests-its-managers-buttons`).

*To close:* the sheet asks what this person may do to this task (the write rule's own answer: edit, comment-level changes as an assignee, or nothing), and draws only those controls, read-only otherwise.

*Measured, lane 5, on `72c5bb7`:* the new suite below, 1 of 5. A member reading an admin's task in a view-only space was offered the title (it opened for editing), the status and the dates, Archive and Delete in the menu, and a comment box, and each change was refused (403) after they made it. The same held in a comment-only space, and on a task assigned to them there. `GET /tasks/:id/capabilities` did not exist (404). Only the space they may edit passed.

ClickUp (help centre, search snippets): "View" is read-only; "Comment" adds comments, and on a task assigned to the person a change of its status; "Edit" changes every task in the location.

*Closed, 25 September:*

- **`GET /tasks/:id/capabilities`** answers what the routes would: `edit` (the write rule at "edit"), `progress` (its status and assignees: the write rule at "comment", which an assignee passes in a comment-only space) and `comment` (the comment rule, now one private method for the route and this answer). A refusal is `false`; anything else is thrown.
- **The sheet asks it with the task**, and shows its loading state until both have answered, so no control is drawn and then switched off. A read that fails, or an answer that is not one (a stubbed API's catch-all), offers what the sheet always did, and the routes still refuse.
- **What it draws by the answer:** the title opens for editing only with `edit`; the status select and its next and complete buttons, the assignee chips and picker with `edit` or `progress`; priority, the dates and their presets, repeat, estimate, the description, Add fields, the type picker, the cover, duplicate, archive, visibility and milestone with `edit`. The menu's Convert, Merge, Custom fields, Archive and Delete are there only with `edit`. The Fields and Checklists tabs sit in a disabled fieldset without `edit`. The subtask rows' controls and their add form, the dependencies' Remove and add form, and the attachments' upload, link and Remove need `edit`. The comment box needs `comment`; without it the tab says the reader may read the comments and not add one (four locales).

### `found-25-sep/task-rows-changed-by-id-anywhere` — **closed** (security, HIGH; found by reading every write that hangs off a task, route by route, after closing `task-sheet-offers-refused-edits`)

**A task's routes changed rows of other tasks by their ids, another organisation's included, and several asked only membership or nothing**

*Measured, lane 5, on `b986949` (probe `measure-task-subwrites`):*
- **Checklists across organisations.** Somebody from another organisation named a task of their own in the URL. With it they renamed an admin's checklist (200) and added an item to it (201). They edited and ticked an item (200). They moved an item into a checklist of their own (200), because the item's update wrote the raw body, `checklistId` included. They deleted an item (200) and a checklist (200). The checklist routes' guard asked about the task in the URL, and the service never matched the checklist or item to that task.
- **Reactions and old descriptions.** The same person reacted to the admin's comment through their own task (201), and its author was notified. They also read the admin's task's old descriptions (200): `GET /tasks/:id/description-history` had no guard at all.
- **A private space.** A member refused a private space still reached a task in it:
  - read its old descriptions (200);
  - saved its checklist as a workspace template, with the items' words in it (201);
  - added a checklist to it from a template (201);
  - cleared its type (200);
  - made a reminder on it, with its title in the answer (201);
  - pushed it to the workspace's calendars (201).

  Each of these asked only for membership of the workspace.
- **A view-only space.** A member in a view-only space made a checklist on a task there (201), ticked an item (200) and changed the task's type (200). Renaming the task was refused (403).

ClickUp (help centre, search snippets): "View" can't comment or edit. A like is a comment-level act. A task's checklists are part of the task, so changing them is editing it.

*Closed, 25 September:*
- **Checklists** are found through the task in the URL. A checklist or item on another task is not found (404). Every change asks the task's write rule: making, renaming, reordering or deleting a checklist, and adding, editing, ticking or deleting an item. The item's update writes only an item's own fields: words, done, position, due date and assignee.
- **A reaction** must be to a comment on the task in the URL (404 otherwise), and it asks the comment rule.
- **A task's old descriptions** are read as the task is (`ResourceMemberGuard`).
- **Templates.** A template can be made only from a checklist its maker may read (404 otherwise). A template's checklist can be added only where the task's write rule allows.
- **A task's type** asks the write rule. The module's other services reach that rule through `TasksService.assertMayEditTask`.
- **A reminder on a task and a calendar push** ask that the task may be read. Otherwise they answer 404, and no title is told.

The new suite `task-rows-by-id`, 6 checks. Every refusal is read back by SQL beside the same act allowed: the admin on their own task, and a member in an open space.
- Before: 0 of 6.
- After: 6/6.

`trb-1..13`, each compiled. Each undoes one rule:
- checklists or items found by id alone;
- the item's update taking the whole body;
- checklists or items changed without the write rule;
- a reaction to any comment, or one asking no level;
- old descriptions unguarded;
- a template made from an unread checklist;
- a template applied, or a type set, without the write rule;
- a reminder or a push on an unread task.

### `found-25-sep/field-values-written-by-readers` — **closed** (security, small; found closing `task-rows-changed-by-id-anywhere`)

**A reader who may not change a task sets its custom fields, and defines new ones**

ClickUp (help centre, "Custom Field permissions", "Use Voting Custom Fields", search snippets):
- A custom field's value is part of the task, changed with "Edit".
- Guests with edit change values and create no fields.
- Anybody who can see a task may vote on it.

*Closed, 25 September:*
- **The task write rule is written once**, in `common/permissions/task-write.ts` (`assertTaskWritable`, and `assertTaskNotInBin`). `TasksService`'s method delegates to it. `CustomFieldsService` could not ask the service's copy, because `TasksService` injects it.

- **Defining, renaming and deleting a field** ask `edit` on the project (and on its list, for a list's field) through `assertSpaceLevel` with the project's chain, so a grant on the project counts. A guest is refused with "Guests cannot define custom fields".

The new suite `field-writes-by-level`, 5 checks, every value and definition read back by SQL:
- A member in a view-only space beside an open one: values, defining from a task and on the project, renaming and deleting.
- A vote in the view-only space.
- A guest with a project shared to edit and a task shared to view.

- After: 5/5.

- values asking the read rule;
- votes asking the write rule;

- guests defining fields.
